title: O thou, my lovely boy: the envoi
short: The last poem addressed to the youth, twelve lines in six rhyming couplets, is generally read as an envoi to Sonnets 1-125.
body: Sonnet 126 is not a sonnet in form: it has six pentameter couplets (aabbccddeeff) and no final quatrain-plus-couplet. It closes the Fair Youth sequence; Sonnet 127 begins the poems on the 'dark lady'. 'Envoi' (from French, a 'sending-off') is the closing stanza or poem that sends a work on its way. 'Lovely boy' is the most direct description of the youth's age in the sequence. The address sums up its themes: Time, Nature, beauty, and the final reckoning.

anchor: Time's fickle glass, his fickle hour
title: Time's fickle glass, his fickle hour
short: The youth holds Time's changeable hourglass and his 'sickle hour'; the archive's second 'fickle' misreads the Quarto's long-s 'sickle'.
body: The 1609 Quarto prints 'times fickle glasse, his sickle, hower': 'fickle' for the glass but 'sickle' for the hour. The archive text reads 'fickle' twice, an error of the kind produced by the long s, which is easily mistaken for f. Editors print 'sickle', Time's reaping hook (compare 'his bending sickle's compass', Sonnet 116), and debate the Quarto comma: 'his sickle, hour' (two separate attributes of Time) or 'his sickle hour' (the hour of death, the reaping hour). The 'glass' is the hourglass and perhaps also a mirror, 'fickle' because it never stays still. The power the youth holds is paradoxical: he seems to have the instruments of Time himself in his hand.

title: by waning grown
short: The youth has 'grown' by 'waning', a lunar paradox: as he ages, his beauty increases while his lovers decline.
body: 'Waning' is the language of the moon. The youth has grown more beautiful by growing older (waning towards death), and thereby 'show'st / Thy lovers withering' (shows by contrast how his admirers, including the poet, are ageing). Booth and Vendler note that the paradox is both a compliment and a warning: what wanes must finally be gone. The rhyme 'show'st / grow'st' underlines the contrast between the youth's growth and others' withering.

title: Nature, sovereign mistress over wrack
short: Nature, ruler over ruin, holds the youth back from ageing as he moves forward in time.
body: 'Wrack' means ruin or destruction (a variant of 'wreck'). Nature is a 'sovereign mistress' who governs decay and can 'pluck thee back' (l. 6) as he 'goest onwards' in time, keeping him young. Her purpose (ll. 7-8) is to show her skill by disgracing Time and killing 'wretched minutes'. The Quarto spells 'minutes' oddly ('mynuit'), which editors normalise. The quatrain stages a contest between Nature and Time in which the youth is merely the instrument of Nature's display.

title: minion of her pleasure
short: The youth is Nature's darling or favourite, but 'minion' also implies a dependent plaything kept at her pleasure.
body: From French mignon, darling. 'Minion' could mean a beloved favourite (often of a monarch) and, pejoratively, a servile dependant; both senses appear in Shakespeare. 'Of her pleasure' means kept for her enjoyment and subject to her will. The warning begins: 'Yet fear her'. The double sense matters: the youth is cherished, but cherished as property, and Nature's favour will last only as long as it serves her. Shakespeare uses the word both affectionately and contemptuously elsewhere, as in Macbeth ('valour's minion', 1.2) and 1 Henry IV ('minions of the moon', 1.2).

title: detain, but not still keep
short: Nature can delay the youth's ageing but cannot keep him for ever; 'still' means always.
body: The verbs distinguish temporary holding ('detain') from permanent possession ('keep'). 'Still' means 'for ever, continually', its usual Shakespearean sense. The youth is Nature's 'treasure', a word that leads into the financial language of the couplet. Nature is imagined as a temporary custodian who must give up what she holds when the debt falls due. The line marks the shift from Nature's apparent power over Time to her ultimate subjection to it, a reversal that the financial metaphor of the final couplet makes explicit and inescapable.

title: audit
short: Nature must eventually render accounts to Time, a creditor, and the youth is the sum she owes.
body: An 'audit' is the formal examination and settlement of accounts. Nature has borrowed time; her account, though postponed, 'answered must be' (must be paid). The bookkeeping metaphor recalls the early sonnets ('what acceptable audit canst thou leave?', Sonnet 4). A pun on 'audit' as hearing (Latin audire) is possible, which the empty brackets that follow would make poignant. The audit is the last of the sequence's many reckonings.

anchor: her quietus is to render thee
title: quietus
short: The 'quietus' is a discharge or receipt clearing a debt; Nature will be acquitted only by handing the youth over to Time.
body: From the Latin formula 'quietus est' ('he is quit', i.e. discharged), written in accounts when a debt was settled. 'Render' means hand over, pay. The word also meant death or release from life, as in Hamlet's 'he himself might his quietus make / With a bare bodkin' (Hamlet 3.1). The last word of the Fair Youth poems is therefore a grim settlement: the youth himself is the payment.

title: The missing couplet: the Quarto's empty brackets
short: In the 1609 Quarto two pairs of empty italic brackets follow line 12, marking where a closing couplet would stand.
body: The archive prints twelve lines only, but the Quarto places two pairs of empty parentheses beneath them, where lines 13 and 14 would be. Whether they were added by the printer (who noticed the poem was short) or reflect the author's design is unknown. Many modern critics read the blank as meaningful: an image of the empty hourglass, the open grave, or a silence after the final reckoning (Duncan-Jones, Burrow and others discuss it). Some editions, following the Quarto, reproduce the brackets.
